So, for fragmentation: fragmentation is an aspect of terminal ballistics. When your bullet strikes a target, it's going to impart hydrostatic shock on the target. The high velocity of the round is actually what makes it so lethal. A 55gr projectile is small, it's barely larger than a 22LR projectile, but it's moving at an incredibly high rate of speed. When something going that fast hits a target at high velocity, it expands rapidly and even breaks apart, fragmenting, and delivering multiple wound channels and doing tremendous damage to medium size game / bipedal predators. This is what makes the 223 / 556 round so lethal. The entire force of the bullet will rip it apart and create multiple wound channels and a large temporary cavity.

For this reason, 556 is most effective at fragmentation range, where it will consistently deliver highly damaging terminal ballistics to targets at close range. You can figure out where your fragmentation range is on your particular rifle by using a ballistics calculator, such as the one found at gundata.org.

On the calculator, you can select your preferred round of choice, eg. Federal 55gr or similar, and then adjust the velocity to match your barrel length. There are various resources to help you determine your rifle's true velocity from a manufacturers' stated velocity, which is usually performed in a 24" barrel down to a 14.5 / 16 / 18 / 20 / whatever type of barrel you are using. Once you've done this, you can set other steps as you prefer, such as your zero height, windage, etc and get a rough order of magnitude estimate of how that round will perform in your rifle. I like to put in an extra variable of a 5 mph 90 degree wind factor just to get an estimation of how a round will perform in average wind conditions.

When you submit the graph, on the output you will see velocities downrange at different distances. When the round starts to get to about 25/2600 fps, thats when the round will reach the end of its fragmentation range. If you hit targets within this range it will perform ballistically with much greater lethality than at further ranges. I hope this is an effective explanation for fragmentation.

World champion shooter Jerry Miculek wears both in-ear plugs and outer ear muffs for hearing protection. It makes for a quieter but much acoustically safer experience. There are two sources of noise in a rifle firing. The first one is the action in the rifle, and the explosion / detonation of the round. The second one is the bullet itself making a "crack" as it leaves the chamber and breaks the sound barrier, like a jet fighter when it floors the throttle. Suppressors only mitigate the first part of the sound equation. Subsonic only mitigates the second part of that equation. As you mentioned, adjustable gas blocks are usually necessary when firing suppressed in order to adjust the amount of gas blowback from the rifle and gas relationship being modified. So in order to get hollywood quiet levels of suppression, you need all three: a suppressor, an adjustable gas block and subsonic ammunition, at least when firing from a rifle / carbine like this.
